classification.difficultyReason: Interpret a secant whose two endpoints move toward the tangency point, then compare how three supplied quotients simplify for a quadratic and a reciprocal.

content.prompt:
[Alternate version]

Draw a clear diagram to illustrate how the following formulae give the gradient of the tangent to $y=f(x)$ at $x=c$.

answer.short: Join $P(c,f(c))$ to $Q(u,f(u))$. The secant gradient is $\frac{f(u)-f(c)}{u-c}$; as $u\to c$, it approaches the tangent gradient $f'(c)$, provided $f$ is differentiable at $c$.
answer.worked:
For $u\ne c$, the secant through $P(c,f(c))$ and $Q(u,f(u))$ has gradient
$$m_{PQ}=\frac{f(u)-f(c)}{u-c}.$$
As $u\to c$, $Q$ approaches $P$. When $f$ is differentiable at $c$, the limiting secant gradient is the tangent gradient:
$$f'(c)=\lim_{u\to c}\frac{f(u)-f(c)}{u-c}.$$
This is the standard formula with $h=u-c$.

spec.description: Authored illustrative curve with a fixed point P, moving point Q, tangent and dashed secant. The source supplies no diagram.
spec.mathematics: Horizontal change u-c and vertical change f(u)-f(c). The secant approaches the tangent as u approaches c when f is differentiable at c.

answer.short: Join $A(c-h,f(c-h))$ to $B(c+h,f(c+h))$. The horizontal change from $A$ to $B$ is $2h$. If $f$ is differentiable at $c$, the secant gradient approaches $f'(c)$ as $h\to0$.
answer.worked:
For $h\ne0$, the secant through $A(c-h,f(c-h))$ and $B(c+h,f(c+h))$ has gradient
$$\begin{align*}m_{AB}&=\frac{f(c+h)-f(c-h)}{(c+h)-(c-h)}\\m_{AB}&=\frac{f(c+h)-f(c-h)}{2h}.\end{align*}$$
As $h\to0$, both endpoints approach $P(c,f(c))$. If $f$ is differentiable at $c$,
$$\begin{align*}m_{AB}&=\frac12\left(\frac{f(c+h)-f(c)}{h}+\frac{f(c)-f(c-h)}{h}\right)\\\lim_{h\to0}m_{AB}&=\frac12\bigl(f'(c)+f'(c)\bigr)\\\lim_{h\to0}m_{AB}&=f'(c).\end{align*}$$
Thus the limiting gradient is the tangent gradient at $P$. The symmetric limit alone does not establish that a derivative exists.

spec.description: Authored illustrative curve with symmetric abscissae c-h and c+h, central point P, dashed secant and tangent. Point coordinates are given in the accompanying editable answer text.
spec.mathematics: The endpoints have horizontal separation 2h. Both approach P as h tends to zero; the differentiability condition is stated in the answer.

children.label: c
children.prompt: Find the gradient of the tangent at $x=c$ for the curve $y=x^2$ using both techniques above, as well as the standard formula. Verify that you get the same answer. Which technique do you think was most convenient to use?

answer.short: All three methods give $f'(c)=2c$. The symmetric formula is convenient because the $h^2$ terms cancel immediately. Other justified preferences are acceptable.
answer.worked:
Standard formula:
$$\begin{align*}f'(c)&=\lim_{h\to0}\frac{(c+h)^2-c^2}{h}\\f'(c)&=\lim_{h\to0}\frac{2ch+h^2}{h}\\f'(c)&=\lim_{h\to0}(2c+h)\\f'(c)&=2c.\end{align*}$$
Part (a):
$$\begin{align*}f'(c)&=\lim_{u\to c}\frac{u^2-c^2}{u-c}\\f'(c)&=\lim_{u\to c}\frac{(u-c)(u+c)}{u-c}\\f'(c)&=\lim_{u\to c}(u+c)\\f'(c)&=2c.\end{align*}$$
Part (b):
$$\begin{align*}f'(c)&=\lim_{h\to0}\frac{(c+h)^2-(c-h)^2}{2h}\\f'(c)&=\lim_{h\to0}\frac{4ch}{2h}\\f'(c)&=\lim_{h\to0}2c\\f'(c)&=2c.\end{align*}$$
All three results agree. The symmetric formula is convenient here because the constant and squared-increment terms cancel, leaving $2c$ before taking the limit. A different preference supported by the working is acceptable.

children.label: d
children.prompt: Repeat part (c) but now with $y=\frac{1}{x}$, and again comment on which technique you think was most convenient to use.

answer.short: All three methods give $f'(c)=-\frac{1}{c^2}$, where $c\ne0$. The formula in part (a) is convenient because $c-u=-(u-c)$ cancels directly. Other justified preferences are acceptable.
answer.worked:
Here $c\ne0$, and all quotients are formed only where their denominators are nonzero.

Standard formula:
$$\begin{align*}f'(c)&=\lim_{h\to0}\frac{\frac{1}{c+h}-\frac{1}{c}}{h}\\f'(c)&=\lim_{h\to0}\frac{-h}{hc(c+h)}\\f'(c)&=\lim_{h\to0}\left(-\frac{1}{c(c+h)}\right)\\f'(c)&=-\frac{1}{c^2}.\end{align*}$$
Part (a):
$$\begin{align*}f'(c)&=\lim_{u\to c}\frac{\frac{1}{u}-\frac{1}{c}}{u-c}\\f'(c)&=\lim_{u\to c}\frac{c-u}{uc(u-c)}\\f'(c)&=\lim_{u\to c}\left(-\frac{1}{uc}\right)\\f'(c)&=-\frac{1}{c^2}.\end{align*}$$
Part (b):
$$\begin{align*}f'(c)&=\lim_{h\to0}\frac{\frac{1}{c+h}-\frac{1}{c-h}}{2h}\\f'(c)&=\lim_{h\to0}\frac{-2h}{2h(c+h)(c-h)}\\f'(c)&=\lim_{h\to0}\left(-\frac{1}{c^2-h^2}\right)\\f'(c)&=-\frac{1}{c^2}.\end{align*}$$
All three results agree. Part (a) is convenient because combining the fractions produces $c-u=-(u-c)$, which cancels directly. A different preference supported by the working is acceptable.
